Side effects and complications associated with biopsy and treatment, including psychological harm and resource implications, are evaluated based on the false-positive rate of the screening test and colposcopy. These are not typically measured in studies but can be estimated. The progression rates of different grades of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) are available from natural history studies. No specific thresholds or treatments are applicable, and the time horizon depends on the interval being considered. 2. Treatment coverage is defined as the proportion of eligible women treated within a population. This is calculated by dividing the number of women completing treatment within a defined time frame by the total number of screen-positive women eligible for treatment in the same time frame, multiplied by 100. The time frame is usually no longer than 12 months. A low treatment coverage increases the risk of invasive cancer detection and mortality, and it reduces the effectiveness of the screening program in lowering cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Data for this metric are collected through an information system or screening registry linking screening and treatment services. No thresholds are set, but higher values indicate better outcomes. The time horizon for this metric is 12 months. 3. The treatment rate refers to the proportion of eligible women treated in a study. It is calculated by dividing the number of women treated by the number of women eligible for treatment. Higher treatment rates improve the likelihood of achieving the desired impact on cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Data for this metric are recorded during the study. No specific thresholds are applicable. Treatment methods include cryotherapy, thermal ablation, large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), and referrals. The time horizon corresponds to the duration of the study. 4. Therapeutic intervention involves treating a diagnosed cervical lesion with the intent to completely remove the transformation zone through ablation or excision, provided there are no contraindications. Diagnostic intervention refers to procedures aimed at obtaining additional tissue for analysis to guide further therapy. 5. The transformation zone (TZ) of the cervix is the area where columnar epithelium has been replaced or is being replaced by metaplastic squamous epithelium. This zone is bounded by the original squamocolumnar junction and the furthest extent of squamous metaplasia, as defined by the new squamocolumnar junction. The visibility and position of the TZ are categorized into three types: Type 1: The entire TZ is visible and located on the ectocervix. Type 2: The entire TZ is visible but has an endocervical component. Type 3: The TZ extends into the endocervical canal and is not fully visible. 6. The squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) is the region of the cervix where the surface squamous epithelium meets the surface columnar epithelium. This junction changes over a woman’s lifetime, and the area between the original and new SCJ undergoes squamous metaplasia, forming the transformation zone. 7. Large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) is an excisional method for treating CIN. A wire loop electrode powered by an electrosurgical unit is used to remove the entire transformation zone, including the lesion and an adequate margin of normal adjacent epithelium (2–3 mm) to ensure a disease-free margin. LLETZ is used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The term loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) is often used interchangeably with LLETZ. 8. Small-loop electrosurgical biopsy involves using a small loop (3–5 mm diameter) for directed diagnostic biopsy, particularly when cancer, microinvasive cancer, or glandular disease is suspected. This serves as an alternative to punch biopsy. 9. Thermal ablation destroys abnormal cervical tissue using extreme heat (≥100°C). Cryotherapy, another ablative treatment, involves applying extreme cold to the cervix using a cryoprobe to freeze abnormal areas. Cold knife conization (CKC) is a surgical procedure that removes the central cervix, including portions of the ectocervix and endocervix, using a scalpel. The amount of tissue removed depends on the size and location of the transformation zone and the likelihood of invasive cancer. 10. Quality assurance in screening and treatment programs ensures consistent accuracy and reliability in detecting and treating cervical abnormalities. Screening registries and call-and-recall systems are essential for organized and opportunistic programs. Strong links between patients and various levels of health services are necessary to ensure continuity and completion of care. 11. Self-collected samples involve patients obtaining vaginal swabs for high-risk HPV DNA testing. This method addresses cultural and logistical barriers to accessing health systems and laboratory-based screening programs. Self-collection kits typically include a single-use swab or cervical brush and a collection/transport medium. The process involves inserting the swab/brush into the vagina, rotating it, transferring it to the collection tube, and sending the sample to a laboratory. Samples remain stable at room temperature for at least 24 hours and, in some cases, for over 30 days. Women generally find this process acceptable, discreet, private, and time-saving. 12. HPV tests use nucleic acid amplification technologies to detect high-risk HPV genotypes. Some tests identify specific oncogenic genotypes, such as HPV 16 and 18, to identify women at the highest risk of developing cervical cancer. Molecular HPV testing detects HPV DNA from high-risk types in vaginal or cervical samples. Tests can either detect high-risk HPV genotypes collectively or distinguish individual types through genotyping. The impact of HPV vaccination on reducing HPV prevalence will influence the predictive values of HPV tests, and recommendations will be re-evaluated as vaccinated women enter the screening age range. 13. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) involves applying a 3–5% acetic acid solution to the cervix to whiten cervical lesions temporarily, producing an acetowhite lesion. This method is suitable for women with a visible transformation zone, typically those under 50 years old. Postmenopausal women often have a receded transformation zone, making it less visible. VIA programs face challenges in maintaining quality assurance, leading to variable sensitivity and specificity. 14. Cytology, including the Papanicolaou (Pap smear) and liquid-based smear tests, examines cervical cells for abnormalities. Cells are collected during a speculum examination using a brush and swab, then placed on a slide with a fixative (conventional cytology) or in liquid storage media (liquid-based cytology). Abnormal results, such as atypical squamous cells of uncertain significance (ASCUS) or lowto high-grade changes, may indicate pre-cancerous changes that could lead to cervical cancer. 15. Colposcopy uses a low-magnification, light-illuminated instrument to examine the cervical and anogenital epithelial tissues. It helps determine the transformation zone type and the grade of suspected epithelial abnormalities. Colposcopy also optimizes biopsy and excisional treatment. Training and supervision are required to achieve proficiency. Traditional colposcopes are free-standing machines, but newer portable models, including those attachable to mobile phones, have improved accessibility. 16. Histology establishes the diagnosis of CIN through histopathological examination of tissue obtained via cervical punch biopsy, endocervical curettage, or excision.
